Importantly, being selected for the scholarship does not end the process. The selected candidate must apply to the Geneva Graduate Institute The scholarship s Steering Committee will help prepare the successful candidate s application file for the Geneva Graduate Institute. The selected candidate must then apply to the Institute by January 15 . The scholarship flyer specifically notes that the late application round does not apply to this process. At this stage, the candidate will need to provide: An English proficiency certificate . Two academic references . These are requested as part of the Geneva Graduate Institute application process. How to Prepare a Strong Application Applicants can improve the clarity of their applications by preparing each component carefully. 1. Research the master s programme Before writing the motivation letter, applicants should identify the specific master s programme they want to pursue at the Geneva Graduate Institute. Applicants should also understand that scholarship selection and university admission are connected but distinct stages. The selected scholarship candidate will subsequently need to apply to the Geneva Graduate Institute and provide an English proficiency certificate and two academic references. Preparing these materials early can help avoid delays later in the process. Application Process The application process can be understood in two main stages. Stage 2: Apply to the Geneva Graduate Institute The Steering Committee reviews applications and selects its candidate. The selected candidate then proceeds with the Geneva Graduate Institute application. That application must be submitted by January 15 and requires an English proficiency certificate and two academic references. Applicants should therefore view the process as a sequence rather than assuming that submission of the scholarship application automatically completes the university admission process. About the Geneva Graduate Institute The Geneva Graduate Institute is a postgraduate institution based in Geneva, Switzerland, with an academic focus that includes international affairs and development. title: The New York Times Local Investigations Fellowship 2026: One-Year Investigative Journalism Opportunity for Local Reporters and Freelance Journalists
summary: The New York Times is offering a Local Investigations Fellowship , a one-year opportunity designed for experienced local reporters and freelance journalists who have compelling investigative story ideas focused on their state or region. The fellowship provides selected journalists with editorial guidance, investigative reporting training, resources and the opportunity to produce significant investigative journalism for publication by The New York Times. The program is intended for journalists who have identified important local issues but may not have had sufficient time, resources or editorial support to pursue them fully. Fellows will work from the communities where they are reporting while receiving guidance from Dean Baquet, former executive editor of The New York Times, and a group of veteran investigative editors. This opportunity is particularly relevant to journalists interested in accountability reporting, public-interest investigations, local government, public safety, health, community issues, institutional failures and other subjects where rigorous reporting can reveal information that has not previously been uncovered. About The New York Times Local Investigations Fellowship The New York Times describes its mission as seeking the truth and helping people understand the world, with independent journalism at the center of its work. The Local Investigations Fellowship supports that mission by giving local journalists the opportunity to develop and pursue substantial investigative projects. Rather than simply providing a conventional newsroom position, the fellowship is structured around a specific investigative reporting idea or area of focus that the journalist wants to explore. Successful fellows spend approximately one year working on investigative journalism focused on their state or region. Their work is expected to result in signature investigative reporting that will be published by The New York Times. The fellowship combines practical reporting with editorial mentorship. Fellows remain based in the communities they cover, allowing them to maintain the local knowledge, relationships and sources needed for effective community-based investigative reporting. Periodic trips to The New York Times offices are also part of the program for training and support. What the Local Investigations Fellowship Offers The fellowship provides selected journalists with an opportunity to develop their investigative reporting skills while working on a substantial local story. Key aspects of the fellowship include: A one-year investigative reporting opportunity focused on a state or region. The opportunity to produce signature investigative journalism for publication by The New York Times . Editorial guidance from Dean Baquet , The New York Times former executive editor. Support from a group of experienced investigative editors. Training in the judgment, skills and techniques required for effective investigative journalism. The opportunity to develop an investigation that may require significant reporting time, records, data and human sources. Periodic travel to The New York Times offices for training and support. The opportunity to bring new perspectives and approaches to investigative journalism. The ability to work from the community where the reporting is taking place. For journalists who have strong investigative ideas but have not had the resources or editorial support necessary to pursue them, the fellowship is structured to provide an environment in which those investigations can be developed in depth. Who Can Apply for the Local Investigations Fellowship? The fellowship is designed for experienced local journalists , including reporters currently working in local newsrooms and independent or freelance journalists. Applicants must meet the basic professional requirements outlined by The New York Times. Basic Qualifications Applicants should have: Three to five years of professional reporting experience covering a beat for a local newspaper or local digital news outlet. Experience as either an independent journalist or a journalist employed by a newsroom that is willing to provide a yearlong sabbatical . Authorization to work in the United States. Applicants should also demonstrate an understanding of and commitment to journalistic independence and The New York Times mission of seeking the truth and helping people understand the world. Preferred Qualifications While not listed as mandatory, The New York Times identifies several qualities that can strengthen an application. Preferred candidates may have: Significant experience covering a particular reporting beat. A well-developed investigative story idea that they have not previously had enough time, resources or editorial support to pursue. The ability to bring new perspectives to investigative journalism. A strong record of reporting stories that demonstrate excellence in writing, news judgment and community-centered journalism. The fellowship is therefore aimed at journalists who already have professional reporting experience rather than individuals seeking their first journalism position. What Kind of Investigative Story Is The New York Times Looking For? A central part of the application is the investigative story idea. Applicants are expected to propose an investigation that could reveal something important about their community, state or region. The proposed story should go beyond simply describing an existing problem. It should have the potential to uncover new information, establish accountability or reveal information that has not previously been made public. The New York Times identifies several characteristics of a strong local investigation. 1. The Investigation Should Start With High Stakes A compelling local investigation should address an issue that has meaningful consequences for people s lives. Applicants should consider questions such as: How does the issue affect people s health? Does it affect public safety? Does it threaten people s livelihoods? Does it affect access to essential services? Does it affect people s quality of life? What are the consequences for the local community? The strongest investigative ideas generally involve issues where the consequences are substantial and where uncovering the truth could make a meaningful difference to public understanding. 2. The Investigation Should Have a Clear Line of Accountability A strong investigation should identify who has responsibility or power in relation to the issue being investigated. Applicants should be able to explain: Who is responsible for the situation? What institution, organization or individual has decision-making authority? What actions or failures contributed to the problem? How can the investigation establish accountability? The objective is not simply to identify a problem but to determine how responsibility can be traced through evidence and reporting. 3. The Investigation Should Reveal Something New The fellowship places emphasis on investigations that uncover information that is not already known. Applicants should consider whether their proposed investigation could: Reveal previously unknown information. Expose a hidden pattern. Uncover records or data that have not been analyzed. Demonstrate a previously undocumented failure. Identify conduct or circumstances that institutions or individuals may not want publicly examined. Provide evidence that changes understanding of an existing local issue. Applicants are encouraged to explain what they believe their investigation could establish and why their reporting could reveal something that existing coverage has not. 4. The Investigation Should Have a Clear Sense of Place Because this is a local investigations fellowship, the proposed investigation should have a strong connection to a particular community. The applicant should be able to explain how the issue is connected to their state, city, region or local community and why the circumstances are distinctive there. The local context could involve: Local government. Public institutions. Health systems. Schools and education. Law enforcement. Courts and the justice system. Housing. Environmental issues. Public infrastructure. Local businesses and industries. Community organizations. Public safety. Local economic conditions. The important point is that the investigation should have a meaningful local dimension rather than being a general national story without a specific community focus. Examples of Investigative Ideas The fellowship description provides examples of investigations that have demonstrated the type of reporting the program seeks to support. One example involved a reporter at The Baltimore Banner who had reason to believe that Baltimore s overdose crisis was the worst in the nation. Another involved journalists at Mississippi Today who had evidence of abuses in local sheriffs offices. A further example involved a reporter at The Desert Sun in Palm Springs, California, who suspected a pattern of deaths inside local jails. These examples illustrate the importance of starting with a specific reporting lead, evidence or pattern and then developing it through deeper investigation. Applicants should therefore avoid presenting only a broad topic. Instead, they should explain what they suspect, what evidence they have already encountered, what remains unknown and what further reporting could establish. Application Requirements Applicants must submit several materials as part of their application. The New York Times specifically requires applicants to upload their: Résumé. Cover letter. Five published reporting clips. These materials must be submitted in one attachment , and applications that do not follow the required instructions or fail to include the necessary materials will not be considered. The five clips should demonstrate the applicant s journalistic ability and should help editors assess the applicant s experience and reporting style. Cover Letter and Investigative Story Pitch The cover letter is a particularly important component of the application. Applicants must include at least one investigative story idea or pitch , although they may include more than one if they wish. Each story idea or pitch should be limited to 500 words . The New York Times states that applicants do not need to submit polished, publication-ready pitches. Instead, the purpose of the questions is to help editors understand the applicant s reporting process and determine what kinds of editorial assistance, resources and support could help develop the investigation. Questions Applicants Should Address A proposed investigation should address the following areas: 1. What is the investigative story idea? Applicants should clearly describe the issue they want to investigate. They should also explain what the investigation could reveal that is not already known. The applicant should consider: What is the central allegation, question or problem? What evidence currently exists? What new information could the investigation uncover? Why is the issue important to the community? 2. Who Has Been Harmed? Applicants should identify the people or communities affected by the issue. They should explain: Who experienced harm? What form did the harm take? How extensive is the harm? What evidence demonstrates the harm? Why is the harm significant? This section should demonstrate that the applicant understands the human consequences of the issue rather than viewing the investigation solely as an institutional or abstract problem. 3. Who Should Be Held Accountable? Applicants should identify the relevant individuals, organizations or institutions that have responsibility or authority. They should explain: Who has the power to influence the situation? What decisions or actions are relevant? What failures or conduct require examination? How could the reporting establish accountability? 4. What Records, Data and Sources Are Needed? Investigative reporting frequently requires extensive documentation. Applicants should identify the critical materials that would be necessary to pursue their investigation, which could include: Government records. Public records. Court documents. Financial records. Internal documents. Public databases. Government datasets. Corporate records. Emails or correspondence. Interviews with affected individuals. Expert sources. Former employees. Current employees. Community members. Applicants should also explain how they have obtained, or could obtain, these sources. 5. What Support Is Needed? Applicants should identify the obstacles preventing them from fully pursuing the investigation independently. These barriers might involve: Lack of time. Limited newsroom resources. Insufficient editorial support. Difficulty obtaining records. Data analysis requirements. Legal or reporting challenges. Geographic limitations. The need for additional reporting resources. Difficulty accessing important sources. The application should make clear why the Local Investigations Fellowship would be useful for advancing the investigation. 6. What Has Already Been Reported? Applicants should demonstrate awareness of existing journalism on their proposed subject. They should explain: What other journalists have already reported. What is already known. What important questions remain unanswered. How the proposed investigation could add new information. Applicants should also include notable reporting clips related to the subject where appropriate. Five Published Clips Required Applicants are expected to submit five published clips that demonstrate excellence in journalism. The clips should showcase abilities such as: Evocative writing. High-impact news reporting. Investigative reporting. Strong storytelling. Community-focused reporting. Effective use of sources. Ability to explain complex issues clearly. Ability to highlight the experiences and voices of local communities. Applicants should upload the full text of their clips , rather than submitting links alone. Choosing the appropriate clips is therefore an important part of the application. Candidates should select work that demonstrates their strongest reporting and provides evidence of their ability to pursue meaningful local journalism. Work Authorization Requirements The Local Investigations Fellowship has a specific U.S. work authorization requirement. Applicants must be authorized to work in the United States . The New York Times states that it will not sponsor new work visas for the fellowship. However, applicants who already hold an existing work visa may be considered. The organization may also consider candidates holding a valid student visa that can be extended through Optional Practical Training (OPT) . This requirement is particularly important for international journalists because meeting the professional qualifications alone does not establish eligibility if the applicant does not have the required authorization to work in the United States. Fellowship Duration and Location The Local Investigations Fellowship is a one-year program . Although the job listing is categorized as remote within the United States, fellows will be based in the communities where their investigations are taking place. The fellowship also includes periodic trips to The New York Times offices for training and support. This structure allows fellows to remain close to the people, institutions and communities they are reporting on while still receiving direct editorial support from experienced investigative journalists. Compensation The listed annual base pay for the position is: $85,262.84 USD per year The job listing states that the annual base pay range for this role is $85,262.84–$85,262.84 USD . For U.S. roles, eligible employees may also receive additional compensation depending on the role, including variable compensation such as an annual bonus and restricted stock. Benefits Depending on eligibility and the specific role, benefits may include: Medical insurance. Dental insurance. Vision benefits. Flexible Spending Accounts (FSAs). Company-matching 401(k) plan. Employee stock purchase plan. Paid vacation. Paid sick days. Paid parental leave. Tuition reimbursement. Professional development programs. The exact benefits available to an individual fellow may depend on applicable employment terms and eligibility. Application Frequency Candidates may apply to the Local Investigations Fellowship once per calendar year . Applicants may also apply for other newsroom opportunities at The New York Times, but they must submit a separate application for each program . This means candidates interested in multiple opportunities should ensure that they complete the required application materials for each individual position rather than assuming one application will automatically be considered for multiple programs. Application Deadline No fixed application deadline is provided in the job listing. Applicants are notified about their status on a rolling basis . The New York Times notes that the fellowship is highly competitive and receives a high level of interest. Candidates should therefore review the official listing and application portal for the current status of the opportunity before applying. The organization also states that it will not accept applications submitted by mail or email. Applications must be submitted through the official application process. How Applicants Are Selected The New York Times states that applicants will be notified on a rolling basis. The organization does not promise to acknowledge every application immediately or provide status updates to every applicant throughout the vetting process. Candidates may be contacted for interviews as needed. Because the fellowship receives substantial interest, applicants should ensure that their submission clearly communicates their reporting experience, investigative idea, evidence, sources, community impact and understanding of the subject. Important Note About Generative AI The New York Times includes specific instructions concerning generative artificial intelligence in its hiring process. Candidates are asked to submit their own work and not use generative AI tools to generate substantive content during the application and interview process. Applicants should therefore carefully follow the organization s instructions and ensure that submitted reporting clips, pitches and other substantive application materials comply with the stated requirements. Union Representation The position is represented by the NewsGuild of New York . This is an employment-related condition identified in the official listing. Equal Opportunity and Inclusion The New York Times Company states that it is committed to maintaining a diverse workforce with people from different backgrounds and experiences. The organization states that it is an Equal Opportunity Employer and that it does not discriminate based on legally protected characteristics, including sex, age, race, color, creed, national origin, religion, marital status, pregnancy, sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, disability, genetic characteristics, citizenship, veteran or military status and other characteristics protected by law. The company also states that reasonable accommodations will be provided as required by applicable federal, state and local laws. Applicants seeking an accommodation during the application or interview process can contact the organization s designated accommodations email address listed in the official vacancy announcement. How to Prepare a Strong Application Applicants interested in this fellowship should approach the application as an investigative journalism proposal rather than a conventional employment application. 1. Develop a Specific Investigation Avoid submitting a proposal that is too broad. Instead of simply proposing to investigate an issue such as public housing, policing, healthcare or local government, identify a specific question, pattern, failure or allegation that can be investigated through evidence. 2. Demonstrate What Is Already Known Research the subject thoroughly and identify existing reporting. A strong application should show that the applicant understands the current state of knowledge and can explain what their proposed investigation would add. 3. Identify the Evidence Think beyond interviews. Consider what records, data, documents and other evidence could establish the facts of the investigation. 4. Establish the Human Impact Explain how the issue affects real people and communities. Demonstrate the consequences of the situation and identify people who can provide firsthand accounts. 5. Establish Accountability An investigative story should have a clear accountability component. Applicants should identify the institutions or individuals whose actions, decisions or failures are relevant to the investigation and explain how evidence could establish responsibility. 6. Select Strong Reporting Clips The five clips should collectively demonstrate the applicant s strongest journalism. Applicants should choose published work that shows their ability to report accurately, write clearly, develop sources and tell stories that matter to local communities. 7. Be Specific About Reporting Challenges If the investigation requires resources that the applicant s current newsroom or freelance work cannot provide, explain exactly what is needed. This could include additional time, data analysis, records research, editorial guidance, travel or other reporting resources. APPLY HERE Important Fraud Warning Applicants should be cautious about fraudulent job advertisements and fake employment offers. The New York Times states that legitimate job opportunities are accessible through its official careers website. The company also states that it will not ask applicants for financial information or payment and will not direct applicants to third parties to obtain employment. Applicants should never send money to someone claiming that payment is required to secure a position at The New York Times. Anyone who encounters a suspected fraudulent job posting or offer can report it to The New York Times using the contact information provided in the official listing. The organization also directs applicants to relevant government fraud-reporting channels. Visit HERE to learn more about the The New York Times Local Investigations Fellowship 2026. Conclusion The New York Times Local Investigations Fellowship provides experienced local journalists with a structured opportunity to spend a year pursuing an important investigative story with the support of veteran investigative editors. The fellowship is centered on producing meaningful local journalism that can uncover new information, establish accountability and give communities a clearer understanding of issues affecting their lives. Applicants should pay particular attention to the investigative story proposal, as the application requires them to explain what they want to investigate, what they hope to uncover, who has been harmed, who may be accountable, what records and sources will be needed, what barriers they face and how existing reporting relates to their proposed work. With a one-year duration, editorial mentorship, investigative reporting support and the opportunity for the resulting work to be published by The New York Times, the fellowship is structured for journalists who already possess professional reporting experience and have a significant local investigation they want to pursue. Applicants should carefully review the official vacancy information, confirm that they meet the U.S. work authorization requirements and prepare all required materials before submitting their application. title: University of Erfurt CEREB PhD Scholarships 2027 in Germany: Fully Funded Doctoral Research Opportunity in Economics and Behavioral Sciences
summary: The Center for Empirical Research in Economics and Behavioral Sciences (CEREB) at the University of Erfurt, Germany , is inviting applications from outstanding prospective doctoral researchers for PhD scholarships beginning in 2027 . The scholarships are funded through the Thuringian State Graduate Support Programme and are intended to support excellent doctoral projects undertaken within the University of Erfurt’s structured doctoral environment. University of Erfurt This opportunity is particularly suitable for researchers whose academic interests lie at the intersection of economics, psychology, behavioral sciences, management, organizational research, decision-making, health communication, corporate governance, business ethics, and related empirical disciplines . Successful applicants can receive €1,400 per month , with additional family support where applicable. The standard funding period is three years , with the possibility of an extension for a fourth year upon application. The application deadline is 24 November 2026 at 11:59 p.m. CET . University of Erfurt About the University of Erfurt CEREB The Center for Empirical Research in Economics and Behavioral Sciences, commonly known as CEREB , is an interdisciplinary graduate and research center based at the University of Erfurt. Its central aim is to bring together theoretical approaches and empirical research methods to investigate important questions about: human behavior; individual and collective decision-making; economic behavior; psychological processes; organizational decision-making; institutional environments; education and life-course development; and social outcomes. CEREB places particular emphasis on understanding how people make decisions, why they make particular choices, how those choices can be empirically studied, and how better decision-making can be facilitated in different social and institutional settings . University of Erfurt The center brings together researchers from different academic disciplines and career stages and operates within an internationally connected research environment. What Does CEREB Research? CEREB s academic profile is strongly interdisciplinary. Research combines theoretical models of human behavior with quantitative and empirical approaches. The center examines decision-making across a broad spectrum, including conventional concepts of rational choice as well as more complex behavioral models involving: bounded rationality; heuristics; context-dependent decisions; social influences; individual differences; organizational structures; institutional processes; and life-course development. Researchers also study how people pursue goals, how different environments affect their choices, and how institutional arrangements influence both individual and managerial decision-making. University of Erfurt University of Erfurt CEREB PhD Scholarships 2027 CEREB is currently seeking excellent PhD candidates who would undertake doctoral research at the University of Erfurt with financial support from a university-administered doctoral scholarship. The wider funding call states that the University of Erfurt intends to award up to four doctoral scholarships using funding from the Thuringian State Graduate Support Programme . The awards are designed to support high-quality doctoral projects conducted within the University s structured Erfurt Doctoral and Postdoctoral Programme (EPPP) through one of its certified Graduate Centres or the Max-Weber-Kolleg. University of Erfurt Applicants interested specifically in CEREB must align their doctoral project with CEREB s academic and research areas. Research Areas Available Through CEREB Successful CEREB scholarship recipients may have opportunities to interact and collaborate with researchers working in several fields, including: Behavioral economics Social psychology Health psychology Organizational psychology Organization and management Corporate ethics Business ethics Corporate governance Individual decision-making Group decision-making Child decision-making Medical decision-making Health communication The broad interdisciplinary structure allows doctoral researchers to develop projects spanning more than one academic discipline, provided there is a clear conceptual and methodological connection to CEREB s research profile. University of Erfurt Scholarship Funding The CEREB-related doctoral scholarship provides substantial financial support for selected doctoral candidates. Monthly Scholarship Successful applicants receive: €1,400 per month as the basic scholarship amount. University of Erfurt Family Allowance Scholarship recipients with dependent children may also qualify for an additional family allowance. The current funding structure provides: €300 per month for the first dependent child €150 per month for each additional dependent child This additional support is provided on top of the monthly scholarship amount. University of Erfurt Research and Travel Support Subject to the availability of funding, doctoral scholarship holders may also apply for support toward research-related expenses. Up to: €600 per funding year may be available for approved research materials and travel expenses. University of Erfurt This could potentially support activities connected with the doctoral project, such as academic travel, research materials, conferences, fieldwork, or similar research-related requirements, subject to approval and applicable funding rules. Scholarship Duration The standard doctoral scholarship period is: Three years However, scholarship recipients may request an extension for: One additional year which means the overall funding period can potentially reach a maximum of four years . University of Erfurt An extension is not necessarily automatic and is subject to the applicable scholarship rules and approval process. Funding Start Date The planned start of scholarship funding is: 1 April 2027 The University specifies that funding must begin no later than: 1 July 2027 . University of Erfurt Applicants should therefore plan their doctoral admission, university enrolment, Graduate Centre membership, and other administrative requirements accordingly. Benefits of Joining CEREB The scholarship is more than a monthly financial award. Successful researchers become part of a structured academic environment intended to support doctoral training, research development, professional networking, and academic career advancement. Scholarship recipients can benefit from: Structured Graduate Programme Candidates have access to a structured graduate programme within the University of Erfurt. This provides a more organized doctoral experience compared with undertaking research completely independently. Research Network CEREB brings together scholars from economics, psychology, management and behavioral sciences, giving doctoral candidates access to interdisciplinary research expertise. International Academic Connections CEREB maintains collaborations with international research institutions and encourages academically rigorous, internationally connected research. University of Erfurt Research Projects Doctoral candidates may become connected with recent and ongoing research projects relevant to the center s areas of expertise. Academic Skills Training The University also provides scholarship holders with access to Academic Skills Training , designed to strengthen research and professional competencies. Science Communication Opportunities Scholarship holders may participate in university platforms supporting the communication of scientific research to wider audiences. University of Erfurt Responsibilities of Scholarship Holders Successful recipients are expected to participate actively in the University s structured doctoral environment. Scholarship holders are generally required to: participate regularly in the programme of their Graduate Centre or the Max-Weber-Kolleg; complete at least six Academic Skills Training courses ; participate actively in academic networking activities; and submit a progress report approximately 18 months after funding begins . University of Erfurt Applicants should therefore view the scholarship as participation in a structured research programme rather than simply receiving financial assistance. Academic Eligibility Requirements Applicants must demonstrate strong academic qualifications and clear research potential. The official funding requirements include above-average academic achievements and examination results demonstrating particular aptitude for academic research . University of Erfurt The selection process particularly considers: previous academic performance; examination results; previous academic or research work; research potential; methodological quality of the proposed doctoral project; academic significance of the research; quality of the research proposal; and feasibility of the proposed work and time schedule. University of Erfurt Applicants should therefore submit a carefully designed PhD proposal that demonstrates both academic significance and practical feasibility. Acceptance as a Doctoral Candidate Applicants must be accepted as doctoral candidates by: one of the University of Erfurt s faculties; or the Max-Weber-Kolleg, by the beginning of the funding period at the latest. That doctoral status must then be maintained throughout the scholarship period. University of Erfurt For CEREB applicants, the proposed doctoral project would normally be associated with the relevant University of Erfurt faculty and CEREB research structure. University Enrolment Requirement Scholarship recipients must also be formally enrolled, or matriculated, at the University of Erfurt by the start of the funding period. Doctoral enrolment is therefore distinct from simply receiving the scholarship or securing the support of a potential supervisor. University of Erfurt CEREB Membership Requirement Applicants whose scholarship application is assigned to CEREB must obtain full membership of the relevant Graduate Centre no later than the beginning of the funding period. Applicants will also need evidence that they have established contact with their intended Graduate Centre during the application process. University of Erfurt Importantly, the official scholarship documentation states that candidates cannot apply simultaneously to several Graduate Centres . Applicants must therefore identify the Graduate Centre most appropriate for their proposed research. Health Insurance Requirement Successful candidates must provide current proof of health insurance by the beginning of the scholarship funding period. University of Erfurt International candidates should therefore take health insurance requirements into account while preparing for doctoral study in Germany. Restrictions on Double Funding The scholarship generally cannot be combined with another source of public funding that covers the same period and purpose. The University specifies that simultaneous funding from other public funds or publicly financed institutions for the same purpose is not permitted. University of Erfurt Funding for research-related stays abroad may nevertheless remain possible where permitted under the applicable regulations. Employment During the Scholarship Scholarship holders can undertake limited paid employment, but restrictions apply. title: Policy & Monitoring Analyst Programme 2026: Join the First Remote CIW Analyst Cohort in Climate Security, Geopolitics and Disinformation Research
summary: Applications are now open for the Policy Monitoring Analyst Programme 2026 , a new fully remote and flexible programme recruiting the first cohort of CIW Analysts . Designed for students, recent graduates and early-career practitioners, the programme offers participants an opportunity to gain practical experience at the intersection of policy analysis, monitoring, climate security, geopolitical risk, information integrity and disinformation research . Rather than functioning only as a training course, the programme is designed around applied work. Selected participants will research and produce original policy and monitoring outputs, collaborate with a core team and develop a professional portfolio that can support future careers in research, policy, international security, geopolitical analysis and climate-related risk work. The programme is particularly relevant for early-career researchers who want to move beyond academic study and begin demonstrating practical analytical experience through tangible outputs such as policy papers, monitoring briefings and data products. Importantly, the programme is described as fully remote and flexible , making it accessible to participants from around the world. The estimated commitment is only 5–10 hours per month , which could make the opportunity particularly suitable for students, recent graduates and professionals who are balancing other academic or employment responsibilities. Application deadline: 6 October 2026. Estimated time commitment: 5–10 hours per month. About the Policy Monitoring Analyst Programme The Policy Monitoring Analyst Programme has been created to provide early-career participants with hands-on exposure to policy research and monitoring in areas connected to climate security and international affairs. The 2026 intake is particularly notable because it represents the first cohort of CIW Analysts . Participants will not simply observe the work of a policy organization. They are expected to contribute to substantive research and monitoring activities while building experience that can eventually be demonstrated to employers, graduate programmes, think tanks, international organizations or other research institutions. The programme emphasizes the growing intersection between two major challenges: The climate crisis Disinformation and information integrity Climate-related risks increasingly interact with politics, security, migration, resource competition, technological change and public information environments. The programme is therefore positioned at a cross-disciplinary intersection where climate policy cannot always be separated from geopolitical or security analysis. For young researchers, this means the work may require thinking across several traditionally separate fields, including: Climate change International security Geopolitics Risk analysis Information integrity Disinformation Emerging technologies Resource conflicts Policy monitoring Why the Programme Focuses on Climate Security Climate security examines the ways climate-related pressures can interact with political, economic and security risks. The programme specifically seeks participants who are interested in understanding these relationships rather than viewing climate change only as an environmental issue. Examples of questions relevant to climate-security analysis may include: How climate risks affect political stability How extreme weather and environmental degradation influence resource competition How climate narratives are used or manipulated in political discourse How emerging technologies affect climate-security decision-making How disinformation influences climate policy How resource scarcity may contribute to tensions between communities or states How governments and international organizations respond to overlapping climate and security risks The programme does not state that every participant will work on all of these questions, but its thematic focus makes these types of policy intersections highly relevant. What Will CIW Analysts Do? Participants selected as CIW Analysts will be expected to contribute actively rather than merely attend lectures or seminars. The programme identifies several major responsibilities. 1. Research and Publish Original Policy Papers CIW Analysts will have opportunities to conduct research and produce original policy-oriented work. This may be particularly valuable for early-career applicants who are trying to demonstrate that they can move from academic reading to professional policy analysis. A policy paper typically requires the researcher to: Identify a relevant policy problem Gather and evaluate evidence Explain the political or security context Analyze developments or trends Present findings clearly Develop conclusions that are useful to policy audiences Producing published work can help participants create a stronger professional profile in competitive fields such as international affairs and policy research. 2. Produce Monitoring Papers and Briefings Monitoring is another central component of the programme. Policy monitoring often involves systematically tracking developments over time rather than conducting a one-time research project. Participants may therefore gain experience in activities such as: Following political developments Tracking climate-security trends Monitoring narratives and information environments Identifying emerging risks Comparing developments across countries or regions Distinguishing significant developments from background noise Producing concise analytical briefings This type of experience can be particularly relevant to careers in: Think tanks International organizations Government policy units Political-risk firms Research organizations Security analysis Humanitarian analysis Climate-policy organizations 3. Produce Data Outputs The programme also states that CIW Analysts may contribute to data outputs . The specific tools or methodologies involved are not described in the call, so applicants should not assume that advanced programming or quantitative analysis is mandatory unless later specified during the selection process. However, data-oriented work could potentially involve organizing, presenting or analyzing information used to support policy and monitoring products. Applicants with experience in areas such as: Excel Data visualization GIS Python R Quantitative research Open-source data Dataset management may therefore have relevant skills, although none of these are explicitly listed as formal eligibility requirements in the information provided. Work Closely With a Core Team Participants will work closely with a core team. This collaborative model means the programme is not framed as entirely independent research. CIW Analysts may have opportunities to learn how professional research teams: Select topics Divide analytical responsibilities Review drafts Exchange feedback Monitor developments Coordinate publication schedules Produce collaborative research outputs For students accustomed mainly to individual essays or dissertations, this type of collaborative work can provide valuable experience. Build a Professional Policy and Research Portfolio One of the programme s clearest objectives is to help participants develop a professional policy and research portfolio . This is especially relevant for early-career applicants because many entry-level roles in policy research ask candidates to demonstrate previous writing or analytical experience. A participant who successfully completes and publishes work through the programme may be able to develop evidence of experience in areas such as: Policy analysis Monitoring Research Briefing preparation Climate-security analysis Geopolitical analysis Narrative analysis Data communication A strong portfolio can potentially complement a traditional CV by showing what a candidate is actually capable of producing. Gain Experience With the Climate Crisis and Disinformation The programme specifically highlights two major challenges: Climate change and disinformation. These subjects increasingly overlap. Public debates about climate policy can be shaped by: Misleading narratives Politically motivated information campaigns False or distorted claims Coordinated online influence Selective use of data Public distrust At the same time, climate-related risks can interact with geopolitical tensions, international security and competition over resources. Participants interested in this intersection may therefore gain experience relevant to an emerging area of policy analysis. Career-Relevant Skills The programme is designed to develop experience relevant to climate-security careers in areas including: Research Policy Risk analysis International security These are highly transferable analytical areas. Depending on the work undertaken during the programme, participants may also strengthen skills such as: Research design Analytical writing Source evaluation Political monitoring Policy communication Trend analysis Critical thinking Collaborative research Structured briefing Evidence synthesis The programme does not guarantee employment after participation, but it is explicitly framed as an opportunity to build relevant practical experience. Main Areas of Exposure The Policy Monitoring Analyst Programme identifies several thematic areas participants may encounter. Policy Research and Monitoring Methodologies Participants will gain exposure to research and monitoring methods used in policy analysis. This is potentially useful for applicants who have studied international affairs or climate issues academically but have limited experience translating that knowledge into professional monitoring products. Climate Security and Geopolitical Risk Climate security sits at the core of the programme. Participants may engage with questions concerning how climate impacts interact with: Political stability Security International relations Economic vulnerabilities State capacity Resource competition Regional dynamics Geopolitical risk analysis requires understanding how developments in one area can affect wider political or security conditions. Emerging Technologies and Climate Security The programme also includes exposure to emerging technologies and their climate-security implications . The call does not specify particular technologies. However, this thematic area could potentially intersect with topics such as: Artificial intelligence Digital monitoring systems Data infrastructure Information technologies Emerging security technologies Applicants interested in technology policy may therefore find the programme particularly relevant. Information Integrity and Disinformation Another major theme is information integrity, disinformation and narrative analysis . Information integrity concerns the quality, reliability and credibility of information within public and policy environments. Participants may learn to examine: Competing narratives Sources of information Patterns of misleading content Political communication Narrative framing Disinformation trends Narrative analysis can be particularly useful in geopolitical and security research because actors often attempt to shape how events are interpreted, not simply what information is available. Resource Conflicts and International Security Dynamics The programme also identifies resource conflicts and international security dynamics as a major area of interest. Climate stress can interact with competition surrounding: Water Energy Land Food Minerals Strategic infrastructure Understanding these relationships may require combining environmental information with political, economic and security analysis. Applicants interested in conflict studies, international relations or natural-resource governance may therefore find this component particularly relevant. Fully Remote Programme One of the programme s most accessible features is that it is: Fully remote. Participants are not required to relocate to another country or city according to the call. This could significantly reduce barriers associated with: Travel costs Visas Accommodation Geographic location The call explicitly describes the programme as accessible to participants from around the world. Flexible Participation The programme is also described as flexible . The estimated workload is: 5–10 hours per month. This is relatively light compared with a conventional internship or full-time fellowship. The programme could therefore potentially be combined with: University studies Graduate research Part-time employment Full-time work, depending on personal workload Other professional-development activities Applicants should nevertheless ensure that they can consistently contribute to the programme. Who Should Apply? The programme is particularly suited to: Students Recent graduates Early-career professionals Early-career researchers Practitioners seeking experience in policy and monitoring Applicants should have a strong interest in one or more of the programme s main thematic areas. These include: Geopolitics Climate security Information integrity Risk management International security Resource conflicts Candidates interested in climate policy, international relations, political risk or strategic analysis may also find the opportunity relevant. Academic Background The call does not specify a mandatory university degree or particular academic discipline . It does not state that applicants must hold a Bachelor s or Master s degree. Instead, it explicitly welcomes students, recent graduates and early-career professionals. Potentially relevant academic backgrounds may include: International Relations Political Science Security Studies Climate Studies Environmental Studies Development Studies Geography Public Policy Economics Sociology International Development Conflict Studies Communications Journalism Data Analysis However, none of these fields is stated as compulsory in the source material. Applicants from other academic backgrounds may therefore still be eligible if they can demonstrate strong interest and relevant analytical ability. Professional Experience The call does not establish a minimum number of years of professional experience. In fact, the programme is specifically designed for people at relatively early stages of their careers. Applicants should therefore not assume that they need extensive professional experience before applying. The programme s portfolio-building emphasis suggests that potential and motivation may be important considerations. International Applicants The programme is described as accessible to participants from around the world . This means candidates are not limited to one country or continent. The remote structure further supports international participation. The call does not specify: Citizenship restrictions Nationality quotas Residency restrictions Applicants globally may therefore apply based on the information provided. Application Requirements The application form asks candidates to provide several basic pieces of information. These include: Name and surname Email address LinkedIn profile CV Applicants must upload their CV through the online application form. The maximum supported file size for the CV is: 10 MB. The form may contain additional sections beyond the portion provided here, so applicants should review the entire application before submitting. How to Prepare Your CV Since applicants must upload a CV, it should be tailored toward the programme s analytical and thematic focus. Relevant experience might include: Academic research Policy writing Research assistantships Monitoring Think-tank work International affairs Climate research Journalism Data analysis Political-risk research Security studies Student publications Model United Nations Debate or policy societies NGO work Applicants with limited formal experience can still highlight substantial academic projects. For example, a dissertation on climate politics or international security could demonstrate analytical ability even if the applicant has not yet worked in a professional policy organization. Strengthening Your Application Although the source does not provide a detailed scoring rubric, applicants can align their materials closely with the programme description. Demonstrate Analytical Curiosity Show that you are interested in understanding developments rather than simply summarizing them. Policy analysis generally requires answering questions such as: Why is this happening? Who are the relevant actors? What are their interests? What might change next? What are the policy implications? Demonstrate Interest in Climate Security Applicants should be able to explain why the intersection between climate and security interests them. Avoid treating climate security as simply another phrase for climate change. A strong application could demonstrate awareness that climate risks interact with: Governance Conflict Migration Economics Geopolitics Information environments Highlight Writing Experience Because participants will produce policy papers and briefings, clear writing will likely be valuable. Applicants should highlight experience producing: Research papers Policy briefs Academic essays Reports Articles Monitoring notes Dissertations Highlight Monitoring Experience Monitoring experience does not have to come from a formal job. It might include: Tracking political developments Media monitoring Election monitoring Climate-data monitoring Conflict tracking Research projects involving longitudinal information Demonstrate Reliability A flexible programme still requires participants who can meet deadlines and contribute consistently. Applicants should therefore demonstrate: Self-management Organization Independence Ability to work remotely Collaborative skills Why This Programme May Be Valuable for Early-Career Researchers One challenge facing students and recent graduates is the gap between academic qualifications and professional experience. Employers in policy and international affairs may ask for: Published writing Monitoring experience Policy analysis Briefing skills Demonstrated subject expertise Yet early-career candidates often struggle to obtain opportunities to develop these skills. The CIW Analyst Programme is explicitly designed around practical, portfolio-building experience , potentially helping participants address this gap. Potential Career Pathways Experience from the programme could be relevant to people considering careers in areas such as: Climate policy Climate security International security Political risk Geopolitical analysis Policy research Think tanks International organizations NGOs Government policy Risk consulting Strategic intelligence Disinformation research Information integrity Conflict analysis Participation does not guarantee employment in any of these fields, but the skills and portfolio developed could be relevant. title: 12 Fully Funded Africa Climate Collaborative PhD Fellowships 2027 at UCT: Climate and Development Doctoral Programme for African Scholars
summary: Applications are open for 12 fully funded PhD Fellowships in Climate and Development under the Africa Climate Collaborative at the University of Cape Town (UCT) in South Africa. The four-year doctoral training programme is designed to develop a new generation of African researchers capable of addressing some of the continent’s most complex climate and development challenges. Rather than following a conventional PhD structure in which candidates move directly into independent thesis research, the programme combines one year of structured pre-doctoral coursework with three years of supervised doctoral research and skills development . The opportunity is open only to citizens of African countries , including African citizens currently living outside the continent. Applicants must already hold a relevant Master’s degree and must be under 35 years old as of 1 February 2027 . Each candidate may apply to only one of the 19 available research topics , and applicants must meet the disciplinary requirements attached to that specific topic. Women and candidates with lived experience of displacement or disability are particularly encouraged to apply. The application deadline is: 15 October 2026 at 23:00 South African Standard Time (SAST). Official Africa Climate Collaborative PhD Fellowship Page About the Africa Climate Collaborative PhD Fellowships The Africa Climate Collaborative is building a doctoral training platform focused specifically on the relationship between climate change and development in Africa . For the 2027 intake, the programme will award 12 fully funded fellowships . Each fellowship is connected to a defined research area and supervisory team at UCT. The broader purpose is not simply to produce additional PhD graduates. The programme aims to strengthen Africa’s research capacity by developing scholars who can work across disciplinary boundaries and produce knowledge relevant to real climate and development challenges. The official call describes the programme as one intended to build a new generation of African scholars addressing the continent’s most pressing climate and development issues. About the Africa Climate Collaborative The Africa Climate Collaborative is a Mastercard Foundation-supported initiative involving several major African and international universities. Its founding partners include: University of Cape Town University of Cambridge University of Ghana Makerere University The Association of African Universities provides coordination. At UCT, the programme is hosted through the African Climate and Development Initiative (ACDI) . The Collaborative works across areas including workforce development, entrepreneurship, research and innovation, and networks, policy and learning. The doctoral programme forms part of a wider effort to strengthen Africa s climate knowledge and skills pipeline and connect young researchers with emerging needs in climate-resilient development and the green economy. Programme Structure: Four Years of Doctoral Training One of the distinctive features of the programme is its structured four-year design. Year 1: Structured Pre-Doctoral Coursework The first year consists of structured coursework . Rather than immediately expecting students to operate independently as doctoral researchers, the programme uses this period to establish a stronger academic and methodological foundation. This is especially valuable for a transdisciplinary programme because participants may arrive from very different backgrounds, including: Environmental science Geography Political science Economics Development studies Anthropology Sociology Engineering Statistics Education Marine science Public health Innovation studies The structured first year is intended to help establish shared foundations for studying climate and development. Years 2–4: Doctoral Research During years two through four, candidates move into: Independent thesis research Supervision by the relevant academic team Doctoral skills training The programme therefore combines formal training with the sustained independent research expected of a PhD. How Many Fellowships Are Available? There are: 12 fully funded PhD fellowships. However, applicants can choose from 19 advertised research topics . This distinction is important. There are more research topics available for application than fellowship places. Every applicant must select one topic only , and multiple applications from the same candidate may result in disqualification. Applicants should therefore choose strategically rather than submitting applications to several projects. 19 Available PhD Research Topics The breadth of the programme is one of its strongest features. Research opportunities cover climate adaptation, cities, health, energy, biodiversity, education, finance, agriculture, water, fisheries and political economy. The 19 advertised research topics are: The politics of care in an African urban flooding-health context Managing locust outbreaks under climate change Whose energy transition? Multi-level governance of electricity commons for implementing the Paris Agreement in Sub-Saharan Africa Who Gets Resilience? Governing Water Infrastructure Investment under Climate Change in African Cities How do knowledge and governance together shape urban climate adaptation interventions in southern African cities? Sustainable concrete technology for African urbanisation An evaluation of energy system impacts (demand and supply) of climate-model-predicted future ENSO swings in Southern Africa Detecting and attributing biodiversity change in the Cape Floristic Region using remote sensing and causal inference Innovation systems and the climate-compatible transition to electric cooking in Africa Innovating equitable, relevant climate and development education in and for Africa Participatory modelling and scenario development for climate resilient fisheries in the southern Benguela From Site to System: a scale-explicit framework for evaluating climate adaptation in South African fisheries Multi-modal remote sensing for smallholder climate resilience: Scaling correlation to prediction and cross-border transferability in sub-Saharan Africa Hydrological reorganisation under climate and development pressures: shifting controls on water partitioning across diverse South African landscapes Building Climate-Resilient Estuaries in South Africa: A Catchment-to-Coast Nature-Based Solutions Framework for the St Lucia Estuarine System Climate-Resilient Blue Bioeconomies: Mapping Indigenous and locally defined ecosystem values contributing to coastal adaptation in South Africa Collective Action for Scaling Business Climate Adaptation How effective is biodiversity spatial planning in preventing habitat loss and supporting climate-resilient conservation? After the policy-bank era: The changing architecture of Chinese power finance in Africa The complete topic list appears in the official call. Topic-Specific Academic Requirements Matter Applicants should not simply select the research title they find most interesting. The programme explicitly states that each topic is connected to a particular supervisor or supervisory team , and the disciplinary background of that team determines the Master’s-level qualifications expected from applicants. Candidates should therefore read the detailed project description carefully and apply only where their academic preparation matches the requirements. This is one of the most important eligibility considerations. Example: Politics of Care, Urban Flooding and Health One of the available projects examines: The politics of care in an African urban flooding-health context. Supervised by Alice McClure in UCT’s Environmental and Geographical Sciences department, the project examines flooding not merely as an infrastructure or environmental problem but through the social and political organization of care. It considers how flood-related health risks are experienced through interconnected systems of household, community and institutional care, including in informal settlements such as Khayelitsha. The project asks questions about: How households manage flood-related health impacts How community networks redistribute care How urban institutions provide or withhold care How different scales of care interact What these dynamics reveal about urban climate-health adaptation Suitable Master’s backgrounds include: Human Geography Anthropology Environmental and Geographical Science Development Studies Urban Studies Sustainability Science Public Health Closely related fields Strong qualitative and ethnographic research skills are particularly relevant. Experience in participatory research, informal settlements, interdisciplinary work or visual and creative methods is advantageous. Ability to communicate in isiXhosa is also listed as an advantage. Example: Managing Locust Outbreaks Under Climate Change Another project focuses on: Managing locust outbreaks under climate change. The project investigates the ecological and climatic processes behind major brown locust outbreaks in southern Africa and how future climate change may affect their location, frequency and intensity. The research will use: Statistical analysis Mathematical modelling Computer simulation Causal analysis Ecological forecasting Adaptive management approaches Applicants should ideally have a strong quantitative scientific background, particularly experience modelling biological systems. Strong programming ability in at least one of the following is expected: R Python MATLAB A strong biological background is also desirable. Example: Energy Transition and Paris Agreement Implementation Another research project is: Whose energy transition? Multi-level governance of electricity commons for implementing the Paris Agreement in Sub-Saharan Africa. The project addresses the relationship between: Energy transition Inequality Climate justice Governance Nationally Determined Contributions International climate obligations It asks how existing inequalities influence regional, national and subnational arrangements for implementing climate commitments and considers how commons-based governance principles could support energy and electricity transitions. Relevant disciplinary backgrounds include: Political Science Sociology Innovation Studies Science and Technology Policy Studies Economics Anthropology Geography Related disciplines The Research Programme Is Highly Interdisciplinary Taken together, the research topics illustrate that this is not a PhD programme limited to traditional climate science. The fellowship portfolio brings climate change into conversation with issues including: Public health Urban inequality Governance Energy transitions Political economy Education Indigenous knowledge Coastal adaptation Agriculture Infrastructure Biodiversity Fisheries Business International finance Development Environmental justice This creates potential opportunities for applicants whose Master’s degrees are not labelled specifically as “climate change,” provided their disciplinary background matches the requirements of their selected project. Eligibility Requirements Applicants must satisfy several important conditions. 1. Completed Master’s Degree Applicants must already hold a: Completed Master’s degree in a discipline relevant to climate and development in Africa. More specifically, that degree must match the disciplinary eligibility requirements attached to the research topic selected by the candidate. This means applicants still completing their Master’s should carefully note that the call specifies a completed Master’s degree. 2. African Citizenship Is Required The programme is open to: Citizens of African countries only. An applicant does not necessarily need to be physically resident in Africa. African citizens currently studying, working or living outside the continent are explicitly welcome to apply. Therefore, eligibility is based on African citizenship rather than current residence . 3. Applicants Must Be Under 35 Applicants must be: Under 35 years old as of 1 February 2027. Candidates should interpret this requirement carefully when determining eligibility. 4. Apply to One Research Topic Only Each candidate may submit an application for only: One of the 19 research topics. The programme warns that submitting multiple applications may lead to disqualification. Candidates should therefore compare the projects carefully before choosing. 5. Successful Candidates Must Obtain UCT PhD Admission Winning the fellowship does not automatically replace UCT’s formal PhD admission process. Successful fellowship applicants must subsequently: Apply for PhD admission at the University of Cape Town; and Be formally accepted by UCT. The programme states that successful fellowship candidates will receive assistance with this application process. This is an important distinction between the fellowship selection and university admission process. Women Are Particularly Encouraged to Apply The programme specifically encourages applications from: Women Applicants with lived experience of displacement Applicants with lived experience of disability These are encouragement and inclusion priorities rather than exclusive eligibility categories. Men are not excluded. Applicants without lived experience of displacement or disability are also not excluded. What Does “Fully Funded” Cover? The official fellowship announcement describes all 12 positions as fully funded . However, the public fellowship page provided for this call does not specify a detailed stipend figure or itemized financial package in the material available here. Applicants should therefore avoid relying on unofficial claims about the exact: Annual stipend Tuition allocation Research budget Medical support Relocation support Travel allowance unless those figures are confirmed through official fellowship documentation. The safest description is that these are fully funded four-year PhD fellowships , while the exact award conditions should be confirmed from the official fellowship offer or programme administrators. Required Application Documents Candidates must prepare several documents. Curriculum Vitae Applicants must submit a CV of no more than: Five pages. The CV must include the names and contact information of: Three referees. At least one of those referees must have supervised the applicant’s Master’s dissertation. Academic Writing Sample Applicants must submit: A sample of previous academic or research writing. The programme indicates that a piece drawn from the applicant’s Master’s dissertation would be particularly appropriate. Applicants should choose a piece that demonstrates: Research ability Academic argumentation Analytical skill Methodological competence Clear academic writing and, where possible, relevance to the selected project. Academic Transcripts Applicants must provide transcripts from: Bachelor’s degree Master’s degree Successful candidates will later be required to submit certified copies before the fellowship is formally confirmed. Letter of Motivation A motivation letter is required. It should explain: Why you are interested in the specific research topic Why you want to participate in the programme How your previous training relates to the research How your experience prepares you for the topic Because candidates apply to one defined research project rather than proposing an entirely independent PhD topic, the motivation letter should be strongly tailored to that specific project. Copy of Identification Candidates must provide a copy of either: National ID; or Passport This is particularly relevant because African citizenship is an eligibility requirement. How to Apply Applicants should first review all 19 research topics and identify the single project that best matches their academic training, research skills and future interests. They should then prepare: CV of no more than five pages Academic or research writing sample Bachelor’s transcript Master’s transcript Motivation letter National ID or passport copy Candidates must clearly indicate which research topic they are applying for. Complete applications must be submitted through the official online application page. Submit an Application Application Deadline The final deadline is: 15 October 2026 at 23:00 SAST. This is a time-specific deadline, not simply “October 15.” Applicants outside South Africa should take the time-zone difference into account and submit early. How to Strengthen Your Application Because candidates can apply to only one topic, the first strategic decision is choosing the correct project. Do not select a project only because its title is attractive. Read the disciplinary requirements carefully and choose the opportunity where you can demonstrate the clearest alignment. Your motivation letter should then explicitly connect three elements: your previous training → the proposed PhD topic → the research contribution you can make. For quantitatively oriented projects, highlight relevant modelling, statistical, programming, GIS or data-analysis experience. For governance and social-science projects, emphasize methodological experience such as: Interviews Ethnography Policy analysis Institutional analysis Participatory research Qualitative coding Political-economy analysis For interdisciplinary projects, demonstrate that you can work beyond the boundaries of your original discipline. The writing sample is also important. Choose a sample that demonstrates your ability to formulate an argument and conduct research independently rather than simply submitting the most recent piece of writing available. Finally, contact referees early. Since the CV must contain three referees and one must have supervised your Master’s dissertation, applicants should confirm their willingness before submission. Key Information at a Glance Programme: PhD Fellowships in Climate and Development Institution: University of Cape Town Programme: Africa Climate Collaborative Host unit: African Climate and Development Initiative Location: Cape Town, South Africa Number of fellowships: 12 Funding: Fully funded Duration: Four years Year 1: Structured pre-doctoral coursework Years 2–4: Thesis research and doctoral skills training Research options: 19 topics Degree required: Completed relevant Master’s degree Citizenship: African countries only Residence: Applicants may live inside or outside Africa Age: Under 35 as of 1 February 2027 Applications per candidate: One research topic only UCT admission: Required after fellowship selection; assistance provided Priority encouragement: Women and applicants with lived experience of displacement or disability CV limit: Five pages Referees: Three, including Master’s dissertation supervisor Deadline: 15 October 2026 at 23:00 SAST APPLY HERE Conclusion The Africa Climate Collaborative PhD Fellowships in Climate and Development 2027 represent a substantial opportunity for emerging African researchers who want to undertake doctoral research at the intersection of climate change, sustainable development and Africa’s social, political, environmental and economic transformations. The programme will award 12 fully funded four-year fellowships at the University of Cape Town. Its structure combines a dedicated year of coursework with three years of supervised doctoral research, providing more structured preparation than many conventional PhD programmes. The 19 available topics demonstrate the breadth of the programme. Candidates can work on questions ranging from urban flooding and public health to climate-resilient fisheries, Indigenous ecosystem values, energy transitions, biodiversity, water infrastructure, climate education, remote sensing, sustainable construction and Chinese power finance in Africa. Eligibility is nevertheless specific. Applicants must be citizens of an African country, possess a completed Master’s degree that satisfies the requirements of their chosen project, and be under 35 on 1 February 2027. Each candidate may apply for only one topic. Applicants should therefore spend significant time selecting the research project that best matches their training before preparing the motivation letter and supporting documents. The programme particularly encourages women and candidates with lived experience of displacement or disability, while remaining open to eligible African candidates more broadly. Applications close on 15 October 2026 at 23:00 SAST. To explore more global opportunities, VISIT HERE .
